chapter_theme: Verses 21 to 40 move from Death and impermanence as the reason to seek release (21 to 24, 37), through faults sorted by mind, speech and body (27 to 29) and an envoy's excellences (26), to the twelve kinds of legal son (30, 31) and rewards in heaven or kingship for restrained speech and for feeding the needy (32 to 36, 40), closing with what is easy and what is hard (39).

21.reading: Youth passes, disease and old age arrive, and wealth and strength wither, so the verse, addressing a woman of milk-sweet speech, says that while one's days remain the rule is to seek release rather than worldly toil.
21.nuance: The verse counts five things, not six: two that leave (youth, and with wealth, strength) and two that come (disease, old age), with wealth and strength sharing one verb; பாடு is read as worldly toil, set against வீடு. வீதி in line 4 is taken as விதி, 'the rule'.

items.claim: youth passes away
disease comes to join one
old age comes to join one
wealth withers
strength withers

22.reading: Death, who does not let one's days run their full count, fears neither sword nor fierce courage, neither beauty nor men nor wealth, and seeing that he comes, the verse says one should take up the book of verse of the one who reached release.
22.nuance: The five things are what a person might use against Death, and each is named only to be refused; the remedy is not a deed but a book, பாவின்நூல், apparently the scripture of the Jina who attained வீடு. ஆம்பொருள் தானஞ்சான் could also be split to include தானம், 'gifts', as a sixth thing Death does not fear; the reading here takes தான் as emphatic.

items.claim: Death does not fear the sword
Death does not fear fierce courage
Death does not fear beauty
Death does not fear men or a following
Death does not fear the wealth one has gained

23.reading: Death regards neither a person's virtue nor his wealth nor his looks, neither a wedding nor an auspicious rite nor the moment, and accepts no guard set at his feet, so the verse calls it beautiful to take the great ones' book as a guard against his mouth.
23.nuance: Six நோக்கான் clauses make the count; கால்காப்பு வேண்டான் is a seventh refusal that turns toward the remedy, a guard (காப்பு) of a different kind, the scripture, closing the mouth that eats. கணம் may be the moment (no right time to die) or a crowd; the reading takes the moment.

items.claim: Death does not regard a person's virtues
Death does not regard wealth
Death does not regard appearance
Death does not regard a marriage
Death does not regard an auspicious occasion
Death does not regard the moment

24.reading: Disease, birth, old age, death, sorrow and unabating want do not hold back, so the verse says the way of release is good if one fulfils it rather than becoming like dancers who play on a decorated stage.
24.nuance: Birth is counted among the evils, not as a beginning: the list is the round of births itself, closed by want. The dancers on the stage are those who play out a life's roles and leave; the image makes worldly life a performance rather than a sin. The count word இவை is fused into நிரப்பிவை, so count_word is left null; the six are counted as written.

items.claim: disease does not hold back
birth does not hold back
old age does not hold back
death does not hold back
sorrow does not hold back
unabating want does not hold back

25.reading: The verse names not frequenting the anklet-wearers and not frequenting the shows that the shareless desire, for once one takes to such shows, enmity, blame, evil talk and death come and do not leave, though they seem to.
25.nuance: The six things are two abstentions and four consequences: the verse sets the cause beside its fruits. பாடகம், the anklet, stands for those who wear it, most likely dancing women; பாத்திலார், 'those without a share', is obscure and may mean men of no settled portion or the women themselves. தீர்ந்தால்போல் தீரா: the harms seem to end and return.

items.claim: not frequenting the anklet-wearers is named as fitting
not frequenting the shows desired by the shareless is named as fitting
enmity comes to one who takes to the shows
blame comes to one who takes to the shows
evil talk comes to one who takes to the shows
death comes to one who takes to the shows

26.reading: For envoys the verse names six excellences: a beauty of mind matured and tested, courage, learning well mastered, power of speech, knowing the time, and fame the world knows.

items.claim: a matured and tested beauty of mind is an envoy's excellence
courage is an envoy's excellence
well-mastered learning is an envoy's excellence
power of speech is an envoy's excellence
knowing the time is an envoy's excellence
fame known to the world is an envoy's excellence

27.reading: Coveting, anger and wrong view, which a person goes on doing even after learning and weighing the warning that they diminish him, are named three faults that belong to the mind.
27.nuance: This verse opens a sequence (27 to 29) that sorts faults by the faculty that commits them: three of the mind here, four of speech in 28, three of the body in 29, ten in all. தீக்காட்சி, 'evil seeing', is wrong view, a doctrinal fault, counted with two passions. கள்ளத்த அல்ல is hard: it may say these are not hidden faults or not deeds of the hand; the reading takes the contrast as mind against outward act.

items.claim: coveting is a fault of the mind
anger is a fault of the mind
wrong view is a fault of the mind

28.reading: Addressing a woman of kohl-dark wide eyes and a peacock's grace, the verse says those who know the truth hold that lying, slander, harsh words and useless words are four faults that come by the mouth.
28.nuance: The four are the faults of speech in the three-faculty scheme begun in 27. மறலையின் is obscure; it may be 'of the wicked' or a form of மறலி, Death, which would make the mouth Death's own; the reading keeps only that the four belong to the mouth.

items.claim: lying is a fault of the mouth
slander is a fault of the mouth
harsh speech is a fault of the mouth
useless speech is a fault of the mouth

29.reading: Killing, theft and a life of burning lust, which the great who stand firm in their vows do not consent to, are named three opposed acts whose rule is that they belong to the body.
29.nuance: It completes the ten faults of 27 to 29 with the three of the body. நிலையளவின் நின்ற, 'who stood in the measure of their station', points to those keeping vows, but the counsel itself is general.

items.claim: killing is a fault of the body
theft is a fault of the body
a life of burning lust is a fault of the body

30.reading: The verse names the first six of the kinds of son that the wise recognise when they take up and protect children: the son of one's own wife, the son of the field, the son of an unmarried girl, the hidden son, the bought son and a sixth whose name is garbled.
30.nuance: These are Sanskrit law-book names of legal sonship (ஔரச, க்ஷேத்ரஜ, கானீந, கூட, க்ரீத, and probably பௌநர்ப்பவ, the son of a remarried woman) in Tamil spelling; with 31 they make the twelve. The verse makes a son a status the household can acquire, not only beget. The identifications are from the Sanskrit names, not from the verse.

norm.note: a classification of legal sonship of the period by the circumstances of birth: from the wife, from the wife by another man, from an unmarried girl, born in secret, bought

items.claim: the son of one's own wife is named among recognised sons
the son of the field, begotten on one's wife by another, is named among them
the son of an unmarried girl is named among them
the son born in secret is named among them
the bought son is named among them
a sixth kind, its name corrupt, is named among them

31.reading: Addressing a woman with the grace of a maddened peacock, the verse names the remaining six kinds of son: the given son, the son taken with the bride, the made son, the son of an appointed daughter, the cast-off son and a son of a sixth kind.
31.nuance: It completes the list of 30 (தத்தன் dattaka, சகோடன் sahodha, கருத்திரமன் kritrima, புத்திரி புத்ரன் putrika-putra, அபவித்தன் apaviddha, and உருகிருதன், perhaps svayamdatta, the self-given). Line 3 runs புத்ரன் and அபவித்தன் together; பொய்யில் may praise the last or the list.

norm.note: the rest of the period's twelve kinds of legal son, sorted by how the boy came to the house: given, brought by the bride, adopted, through a daughter, found abandoned

items.claim: the given son is named among the remaining kinds
the son brought with the bride is named among them
the made son is named among them
the son of an appointed daughter is named among them
the cast-off son taken in is named among them
a sixth kind, perhaps the self-given son, is named among them

32.reading: One who does not speak of his own lineage and family standing, does not speak of others' defects, does not speak of his wealth, his way of life or his span of years, and who gives before he eats, is to be known, the verse says to a woman of bee-sought tresses, as god of gods.
32.nuance: Five of the six restraints are silences about oneself (birth, standing, wealth, life, age); the one about others is not to name their defects. The reward is given to the giver, ஈத்துண்பான், so the silences frame the giving.

items.claim: not speaking of one's lineage
not speaking of one's family standing
not speaking of others' defects
not speaking of one's wealth
not speaking of one's way of life
not speaking of one's span of years

33.reading: One who does not lie, does not revile, does not backbite, speaks truth to everyone, speaks openly of what he has and does not speak to wound will, the verse says to a peacock-like woman, leave this world and become king of the assembled gods.
33.nuance: All six are about speech; உள்ளனவும் விட்டுரையான் is read as one who does not hide what he has from those who ask, which joins speech to giving. எய்யுரையான் is uncertain: 'not speaking words that pierce' or 'not mocking'.

items.claim: not lying
not reviling
not backbiting
speaking truth to all
speaking openly of what one has
not speaking to wound

34.reading: One who does not speak destructive words or speak in hatred, has no anger, does not proclaim his own nature, does not speak of baseness, and gives what fits to those who want it is, the verse says to a woman with lips red as the kovvai fruit, sought with love by the gods.
34.nuance: Verses 32 to 34 form a run: restraint of speech joined to giving, rewarded each time in heaven, rising from god of gods to king of the gods to sought by the gods. The fruit is put in the gods' wish, not in his merit.

items.claim: not speaking destructive words
not speaking in hatred
having no anger
not proclaiming one's own nature
not speaking of baseness
giving what fits to those who want it

35.reading: One who gives blameless food as their share to renouncers and to those not renounced, to the powerless, the unseen, the bereaved, the destitute and the young, and to the excellent as well, will, the verse says to a woman of musical speech, rule the earth as king.
35.nuance: The recipients run to eight, not six: the verse adds சிறந்தவர்க்கும், 'to the excellent too', after the needy, so the list closes by widening, not narrowing. தோன்றார் may be those who keep out of sight (the shamed poor), and இறந்தார் those whose support has died; துறவாதார் may be householders in need. பாற்படுத்தான், 'set as a share', makes the gift a portion due, not a favour.

items.claim: giving food to renouncers
giving food to those who have not renounced
giving food to the powerless
giving food to those who do not show themselves
giving food to the bereaved
giving food to the destitute
giving food to the young
giving food to the excellent as well

36.reading: Those who prepare a deeply satisfying meal for the lame, the blind, the mute, those with no kin at all and those with no learning to hold to will swiftly, the verse says, be desired by the gods.
36.nuance: The count is five: three bodily lacks, then a social lack (no kin) and a lack of learning, so the unlearned are set among the disabled as people owed food. சாலவும் ஆழப் படும் is taken with the meal ('filling deeply'); read as 'those deeply sunk in need' it would make a sixth.

items.claim: feeding the lame
feeding the blind
feeding the mute
feeding those with no kin at all
feeding those with no learning to hold to

37.reading: Death does not go away when people weep, does not fear, does not listen when they cry out, does not leave for the helpless, does not go away when they worship, and regards no worth, so the verse calls it a failing to sit idle without striving at penance.
37.nuance: Each item is a plea that fails (tears, threats, cries, helplessness, worship), so worship itself is counted among the useless defences; only தவம், practised beforehand, is set against Death. The six are actions Death refuses, not things.

items.claim: Death does not leave when one weeps
Death does not fear
Death does not listen to cries
Death does not rise and leave
Death does not leave when worshipped
Death regards no worth

38.reading: The great penance of those who fully understand that one does not reach it except by noble conduct is something not removed by letters, not ended by numbers, not altered by praise and hymns, and failing to go that way is utter baseness.
38.nuance: The verse sets penance against three learned or ritual substitutes, script, number (counting or astrology) and praise, and makes conduct the only road. புலை here is baseness, not a caste term. The syntax is compressed and the subject of the three negatives may instead be the bond of deeds that penance alone removes.

items.claim: it is not removed by letters
it is not ended by numbers
it is not altered by praise and hymns
it is reached only by noble conduct

39.reading: Dying is easy and fullness of character hard; to reach for the good is easy and to guard truth hard; to go toward what will be is easy and to stand firm hard; to win by being clever is easy and the right word hard.
39.nuance: Four easy-and-hard pairs make eight things; each hard thing is the lasting form of its easy partner. Putting death among the easy things reverses the death verses earlier in the chapter. The last pair ranks speech above victory; (எளிது) in line 2 is an editorial restoration.

items.claim: dying is easy
fullness of character is hard
reaching for the good is easy
guarding truth is hard
going toward what will be is easy
standing firm is hard
winning by cleverness is easy
the right word is hard

40.reading: Not wavering, hastening to what has befallen others, not tormenting living beings, not doubting, choosing the way that ends impermanence, and removing hunger where it is found make one whose gaze is on the heights of heaven.
40.nuance: The list joins inner steadiness (not wavering, not doubting), care (running to help, removing hunger), non-harm and the choice of release, so feeding the hungry stands beside the way out of impermanence. The division of line 1 is uncertain: உற்றதற்கு ஓடி may go with உலையாமை ('not shaken by what befalls').

items.claim: not wavering
hastening to what has befallen
not tormenting living beings
not doubting
choosing the way that ends impermanence
removing hunger where it is found

links.note: Naladiyar 53 counts goods that fail (home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth, strength) as the reason to renounce; Elathi 21 counts the same failing goods together with what arrives, disease and old age.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show that the case for release can be argued from loss alone or from loss and arrival, and Elathi's version gives the body's afflictions equal weight with the goods that slip away.
links.list_adds: It pairs what leaves with what comes in one list of five, so the argument moves from fading goods to arriving afflictions, which the quatrain does not count.

links.note: Naladiyar 52 has the best reflect on impermanence, disease, old age and death and do their own work; Elathi 24 lists disease, birth, old age, death, sorrow and want and names the work as the way of release.
links.teaches: Read together, the quatrain's unnamed 'own work' is given a name and its four evils gain birth and want, so the round of births itself becomes the thing to escape.
links.list_adds: It adds birth and unending want to the Naladiyar's four, making the list the cycle of births rather than the ills of one life.

links.note: Both verses list what Death disregards and close with a book as the remedy; 22 names the defences Death does not fear, 23 the occasions and qualities he does not look at.
links.teaches: Together they show the chapter's argument that no strength, wealth, virtue or auspicious time stops Death, and that the Jain answer in both is scripture, not effort or rite.

links.note: Kural 686 names the envoy as learned, fearless of hostile eyes, persuasive and knowing the time; Elathi 26 has the same four and adds a tested beauty of mind and fame known to the world.
links.teaches: The pair shows the envoy's qualities carried from the Kural into a later list that makes reputation itself a qualification, so the envoy is chosen partly for being known.
links.list_adds: It sets world-known fame as a sixth excellence beside the Kural's four, ranking renown with skill as something an envoy must already have.

links.note: Kural 35 defines virtue as avoiding envy, craving, anger and harsh speech, mixing faults of mind and of speech in one four; Elathi 27 names three faults (coveting, anger, wrong view) and assigns them to the mind alone.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the Kural's single list is seen sorted in Elathi by the faculty that sins, and wrong view, a doctrinal error, enters a list the Kural keeps to passions.
links.list_adds: It sorts faults by faculty, mind here and speech and body in the next two verses, and adds wrong view to the passions, a sorting the couplet does not make.

links.note: Kural 360 names desire, anger and confusion as the three whose end ends pain; Elathi 27 names coveting, anger and wrong view as the three faults of the mind.
links.teaches: Both books build a triad of inner faults with anger at its centre, but where the Kural ends in confusion, a lack of seeing, Elathi ends in wrong view, a positive false belief, which shows the Jain stress on right doctrine.
links.list_adds: It replaces confusion with wrong view and puts the triad inside a scheme of ten faults across mind, speech and body.

links.note: 27 names three faults of the mind, 28 four faults of the mouth.
links.teaches: Read in sequence, the two verses (with 29) show the work laying out a full ten-part scheme of faults by faculty, mind three, speech four, body three, spread over consecutive verses.

links.note: 29 names three faults of the body and closes the scheme begun in 27 and continued in 28.
links.teaches: With 29 the ten faults are complete, and the pairing shows that the counting form can carry one doctrine across several verses rather than finishing in each.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 18 lists not lying, not stealing, not desiring women and not eating flesh as what ends rebirth; Elathi 29 names killing, theft and lust as the body's faults.
links.teaches: Taken together, Elathi's body-faults are seen in Sirupanchamoolam as conditions of escaping rebirth, and the sister Jain work adds flesh-eating to the bodily code Elathi frames by faculty.

links.note: 30 names six kinds of legal son and 31 names the remaining six.
links.teaches: Only read together do the two verses give the twelve kinds of son of the law-books, showing the work importing a Sanskrit legal classification whole into Tamil verse.

links.note: Kural 50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived is placed among the gods; Elathi 32 says one who keeps six silences about himself and others and gives before eating is god of gods.
links.teaches: The pair fills the Kural's undefined 'as life should be lived' with particular restraints of speech and the act of giving, and raises the reward from a place among the gods to their head.
links.list_adds: It spells out the good life as six named silences, mostly about one's own birth, wealth and years, joined to giving before eating.

links.note: Kural 86 says the host who tends guests will be a welcome guest to the gods; Elathi 34 says the gods seek with love one who gives what fits and keeps from angry and boastful speech.
links.teaches: Both books put the giver's reward in the gods' welcome, and Elathi adds that restraint of speech and anger, not hospitality alone, is what the gods are drawn to.
links.list_adds: It sets the giving beside five restraints of speech and temper, so the gift alone does not earn the welcome.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 70 promises kingship to those who give to prisoners and to people keeping fasts; Elathi 35 promises rule of the earth to one who gives food to renouncers, the needy and the young.
links.teaches: The two Jain lists share the reward of kingship for feeding, but Sirupanchamoolam's recipients are mostly ascetics fasting by rule while Elathi's are mostly the needy, which shows the same promise attached to two different kinds of worthy receiver.

links.note: Kural 226 calls removing the hunger of the destitute the place to store wealth; Elathi 36 names whom to feed (the lame, the blind, the mute, the kinless, the unlearned) and says the gods will desire such givers.
links.teaches: The pair turns the Kural's general 'destitute' into named kinds of person who cannot earn, and moves the giver's return from stored wealth to the gods' regard.
links.list_adds: It names five kinds of need, bodily, social and of learning, and puts the unlearned among the disabled as people owed food.

links.note: Kural 335 says to hurry to good deeds before the death rattle stops the tongue; Elathi 37 lists the pleas Death ignores, worship among them, and names penance as the remedy.
links.teaches: Together they show the urgency of the Kural's couplet sharpened into a Jain argument in which even worship fails before Death and only penance done in time avails.
links.list_adds: It counts six failed appeals to Death, including worship, so ritual is set aside before penance is named.

links.note: Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle endlessly of grammar and astrology the greatest fools; Elathi 38 says the great penance is not removed by letters, numbers or hymns but reached by conduct.
links.teaches: Read together, both Jain works set letters and number-lore against the real work, and Elathi names that work as conduct within penance where the quatrain leaves it as one's own task.
links.list_adds: It puts praise and hymns beside letters and numbers as three substitutes for conduct, adding the devotional to the learned ones the quatrain mocks.

links.note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy and doing as spoken is hard; Elathi 39 lists four easy-hard pairs and ends that winning is easy and the word is hard.
links.teaches: The same easy-hard form ranks speech oppositely in the two books, because Kural 664 means announcing a plan while Elathi means the right and truthful word, so the pair shows how much 'speech' changes with what kind of speaking is meant.
links.list_adds: It sets four easy-hard pairs in a row, death against character and victory against the word, so speech is ranked among the hard things the Kural keeps for deeds.

links.note: 37 treats Death as the overpowering thing no plea escapes; 39 calls dying easy beside the hard work of character.
links.teaches: Within one chapter the work views death from two sides, as the terror that drives penance and as the easy thing beside lasting virtue, and the pair shows death's weight depends on what it is measured against.

links.note: Naladiyar 92 sets death, age and disease before the reader and urges sharing food while wealth is in hand; Elathi 40 joins choosing the way out of impermanence with removing others' hunger.
links.teaches: Together they show the ethics group tying the feeding of the hungry to the escape from impermanence, and Elathi places it among inner disciplines like not doubting and not wavering.
links.list_adds: It sets removing hunger beside non-harm, steadiness and the choice of release, so feeding becomes one of the marks of one bound for heaven.

source_issues: 24 line 1: புறப்பு is most likely a misprint for பிறப்பு (birth).
30 line 3: ஓளரதனே looks like a misspelling of ஔரசன் (aurasa); line 4: கிரிதன்பென கற்பவன் appears corrupt, probably கிரிதன் and a garbled பௌனர்ப்பவன்.
31 line 3: புத்ரனப வித்தனோடு runs புத்ரன் and அபவித்தன் together with a broken word division.
34 lines 1-2: உரைய and உரையாள் look like misprints for உரையான், matching the other clauses.
39 line 2: (எளிது) is an editorial restoration in parentheses, not in the verse as transmitted.
29 line 3: மையெனநீள் கண்ணாய் is spelled as one run; the address is clear but the division is editorial.
